newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Deutsche to compensate MGAM victims.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Deutsche to compensate MGAM victims.

text.p: Germany's Deutsche Bank AG on Monday said it would be forced to pay out compensation to investors hurt by the crisis in September at its London funds unit, Morgan Grenfell Asset Management.

But the bank dismissed as "pure speculation" a report in the Guardian newspaper that it would have to repatriate 200 million pounds ($337 million) to make good investors' losses, saying London regulatory body IMRO was still calculating the amount due.
"We have already informed investors that compensation will be paid. This is something that is still being investigated and we have no definitive figure," a bank spokesman told Reuters.

The spokesman also dismissed as speculative the Guardian's assertion that IMRO would impose a record-breaking one-million pound fine over the incident. He added that he was not sure when IMRO would release its report on the issue.
A Deutsche board member said recently he expected IMRO to decide on the issue of compensation by the end of the year.
The bank's share price was hurt by the report, with its stock ending bourse trade in Frankfurt down 40 pfennigs at 72.90 marks, bucking the broader market's upward trend.

Deutsche has already injected 180 million sterling into MGAM after three of the unit's European funds had to be temporarily suspended in September pending an investigation into the valuation of unlisted speculative stocks they contained.

The bank, Germany's largest, has since dismissed the fund manager at the centre of the crisis, Peter Young, and four more top level managers. The funds concerned, held by some 90,000 retail investors, resumed trading after Deutsche's cash injection.

In an unsourced report on Saturday, the Guardian said the total cost of the MGAM debacle would be some 400 million pounds, and that IMRO planned to force the bank to "make good every penny of investment returns."
Deutsche's spokesman said IMRO's investigations into the MGAM saga were not yet completed so that any mention of specific levels of compensation was "pure speculation."
"The size of the compensation will be determined on the basis of IMRO's objective calculations," he said, declining to project how high that compensation might be.
Both IMRO (Investment Management Regulatory Authority) and the Serious Fraud Office (SFO) are probing the MGAM incident.
Meanwhile, Deutsche has opted to keep a closer eye on MGAM's unit trust business in future.
Last month, the bank said its German DWS asset management unit would take direct control from Frankfurt of MGAM's retail client business.
